findings.title: enableSqlExpressions has unreachable logic and silently neutralises the feature toggle
findings.body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` from both the `if enabled` branch and the fall-through, so the function is a constant `false` and the feature-flag lookup is completely dead. The negation is also inverted relative to the variable name (`enabled` is true when the flag is *off*), which makes the code read as a logic error rather than an intentional kill switch. Consequences: (a) the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle no longer has any effect on this code path, which is surprising for anyone later trying to re-enable the feature by flipping the flag; (b) static analysis/lint (ineffectual assignment, identical branch returns) is likely to flag it. If the intent is a hard disable, the function should simply `return false` with a comment explaining why, or the type case should return the error directly.

findings.title: User-facing error says "not implemented" while the sqlExpressions toggle is still registered and documented
findings.body: Requests of `QueryTypeSQL` are now rejected with `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. The `sqlExpressions` feature toggle remains registered in featuremgmt and documented as an available (experimental) flag, so an operator who enables it, and users who already have saved SQL expression queries, will get an error that contradicts the documentation and gives no hint that the feature was deliberately removed/disabled for security reasons. Either the toggle/docs should be marked as unavailable, or the message should state that SQL expressions are currently disabled.

findings.title: Feature gate only added to the new reader path; legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path relies solely on the stubbed DB
findings.body: The explicit disable check was added only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` (pkg/expr/reader.go). The other entry point, `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` (used by the classic/non-apiserver expression pipeline), has no toggle or disable check at all; it is only prevented from working because `sql.DB.RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` in the new `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` stub return `errors.New("not implemented")`. If `sql.DB` is ever re-implemented (which is the obvious next step for this package), that path silently becomes reachable again with no gate, re-opening the vulnerable surface. The gate should be applied at command construction/execution as well, not just in the query reader. Additionally, every such request now takes the `logger.Warn("invalid sql query", "sql", rawSQL, ...)` branch and surfaces an opaque `error reading SQL command` BadRequest, which both logs user-supplied query text on every attempt and gives no indication the feature is disabled.

findings.title: No test asserts that SQL expressions are rejected
findings.body: This change is a security fix that disables a code path, but no test is added or updated. There is nothing verifying that `ReadQuery` returns an error for `QueryTypeSQL` (with the toggle both on and off), nor that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail safely against the new stub `sql.DB`. Without such a test, a future refactor (e.g. "fixing" the obviously odd `enableSqlExpressions` helper, or implementing `sql.DB`) can silently re-enable the vulnerable path with a green CI.

findings.title: tablesFromAST indexes ast[0] without a length check
findings.body: `tablesFromAST` does `flatten.Flatten(ast[0], ...)` immediately, so an empty JSON array (`[]`) returned from the serialization step causes an index-out-of-range panic. Today this is unreachable because `DB.RunCommands` is a stub that always errors, but the DuckDB-specific code in `TablesList` (the `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` command, the single-quote escaping) is left in place and will be the starting point if/when a real backend is wired up again. Either add a length guard, or remove this now-dead DuckDB-specific parser along with the dependency it was built for so it cannot be reactivated by accident.
